items.prose: A calibrated model gives $p = 0.8$ that a trade wins.
items.question: What is the AFML bet size, $2\Phi(z) - 1$ with $z = (p - \tfrac12)/\sqrt{p(1-p)}$? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: A 0.8 call gets a little over half the full size.

byKey.kelly: That is Kelly at even odds, $2p - 1$. The AFML curve is lower.

items.prose: A trade wins £1.50 per £1 staked with probability 0.5, and loses the £1 otherwise.
items.question: What fraction does Kelly stake? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: A coin flip that pays 3 to 2 is worth a sixth of capital.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $f = p - (1 - p)/b$ with $b = 1.5$.

byKey.even: You used the even-odds rule $2p - 1$. A win pays £1.50, so the edge is positive.
byKey.times: You multiplied the loss term by $b$. Divide it: $0.5/1.5$.

explain.text: $f = 0.5 - 0.5/1.5 = 0.5 - 0.333 = 0.167$. Even at $p = 0.5$ the better payout makes a bet worthwhile.

items.prose: A signal earns 4 bp a day gross with turnover 0.5.
items.question: What is its break-even cost a side, in bp?

feedback.correct: Each unit traded carries 8 bp of edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the gross per day by the turnover.

byKey.times: You multiplied. The edge per unit traded is gross divided by turnover.

explain.text: Half a unit trades each day to earn 4 bp, so each unit carries $4/0.5 = 8$ bp. Costs above 8 bp a side make the signal lose.

items.prose: A book has daily turnover 0.3 and pays 12 bp a side.
items.question: What do costs take per year, as a percentage of the book? Use 252 days.

feedback.correct: About 9% a year, before any edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply turnover, days and cost per unit.

byKey.daily: That is one day's cost. Multiply by 252.
byKey.no-turn: You charged a full unit every day. Turnover is 0.3.

explain.text: $0.3 \times 252 = 75.6$ units a year, at 0.12% each: 9.07%. The gross edge must beat that before anything is earned.

items.prose: A monthly strategy has a Sharpe of 0.2 a month over 48 months, with skew −1 and kurtosis 6.
items.question: What is the standard error of its Sharpe ratio? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Skew and tails add about 11% to the error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $1 - \gamma_3 SR + \tfrac{\gamma_4 - 1}{4}SR^2$, divide by $n - 1$, take the root.

byKey.normal: That ignores skew and kurtosis. With $\gamma_3 = -1$ the error is wider.
byKey.excess: You used kurtosis 6 as excess kurtosis, adding 3 more. The formula takes the full kurtosis, here 6.

explain.text: The top is $1 + 0.2 + 1.25 \times 0.04 = 1.25$, so the error is $\sqrt{1.25/47} = 0.163$, against 0.147 for normal returns.

items.prose: A study's DSR is 0.88. The researcher wants it higher.
items.question: Which change raises the DSR honestly?

options.text: Try 20 more variants and keep the best
options.why: More trials raise $E[\max]$ and lower the DSR of any given Sharpe. Keeping the best only looks better.

options.text: Wait for more out-of-sample data on the same fixed rule
Report only the 3 variants that worked
options.why: The 3 shown were chosen from more. The trial count is what was tried.

options.text: Count every overlapping daily return as an observation
options.why: That shrinks the standard error falsely. Use the effective number of observations.

feedback.correct: More data on a fixed rule is the honest route.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which option changes the evidence rather than the accounting?

explain.text: A longer record of the same rule shrinks the standard error with no new trials. The other options either add trials or hide them.

items.prose: A trial log holds: logistic C = 1; logistic C = 0.1; logistic C = 1 (rerun); boosting depth 2; boosting depth 3; boosting depth 2 (rerun).
items.question: What trial count goes into the DSR?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count distinct configurations, each once.

byKey.runs: You counted runs. A rerun of the same configuration is not a new trial.
byKey.models: You counted model families. Each setting tried is its own trial.

explain.text: Distinct configurations: logistic at C = 1 and 0.1, boosting at depth 2 and 3. Four trials.

items.prose: A model says $p = 0.65$ on even-odds trades, but calibration shows they win 58% of the time. The desk sizes by Kelly from the model and pays costs on every change.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: It bets about twice the true Kelly, and its larger, jumpier positions also pay more cost
Sizing does not matter; only costs do
options.why: Sizing matters: Kelly from 0.65 is 0.3, the true Kelly 0.16. Nearly double, where growth is about zero.

options.text: Overconfidence is safe because Kelly is conservative
options.why: Kelly is the growth peak, not a safe level. Above it growth falls fast.

options.text: Calibration only matters for accuracy, not for P&L
options.why: Size is a function of $p$. A wrong $p$ is a wrong size, which is a wrong P&L.

feedback.correct: An overconfident $p$ costs twice: in size and in turnover.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare Kelly from 0.65 with Kelly from 0.58.

explain.text: Kelly from the model is $2 \times 0.65 - 1 = 0.3$; from the truth, 0.16. Near twice Kelly, growth is about zero, and the bigger positions trade more units, so costs are higher too.

items.prose: The lesson's seed-7 study had a net Sharpe of 0.28 over 271 days with 2 trials, DSR 0.41. Suppose the trial log had shown 10 configurations instead. Assume normal returns.
items.question: What would the DSR be? Give 2 decimal places.

widget.label: DSR
widget.accept: 0.10: $E[\max]$ for 10 trials is $1.575/\sqrt{270} = 0.0958$ a day, against a daily Sharpe of 0.0174.

feedback.correct: With 10 trials the result is almost surely luck.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise the benchmark to $E[\max]$ for $N = 10$ and $V = 1/270$.

byKey.two: That is the DSR with 2 trials. With 10 the benchmark rises.
byKey.psr: That is close to the PSR against zero. The DSR benchmark is the best of 10 noise trials.

explain.text: Daily Sharpe $0.2757/\sqrt{252} = 0.0174$; $E[\max] = 0.0958$; standard error about 0.061. So $z = -1.29$ and DSR $= 0.10$. The trial count can turn weak evidence into none.
